extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in geometric analysis / Ricci flow
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, conditions and estimates governing injectivity radius bounds, classification of maximal Ricci-flow solutions (Type I/II/III), definitions of (almost) maximum points and injectivity-radius conditions, and characterization/construction of singularity model limits (including Ricci soliton identifications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheeger's Lemma (injectivity radius lower bound for compact manifolds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let M be an n-dimensional compact Riemannian manifold with Vol(M) ≥ λ, diameter d(M) ≤ D, and sectional curvature bounded |K_M| ≤ v. Then inj(M) ≥ C_n(λ, D, v) for some positive constant depending only on λ, D, v and n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an injectivity-radius estimate for compact manifolds that does not impose a sign restriction on sectional curvature; constant Cn depends only on the listed global geometric quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheng–Li–Yau localized injectivity radius estimate (Theorem 4.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description:
Let B(x0,4r0) be a geodesic ball in an n-dimensional complete Riemannian manifold (M,g) with sectional curvature K satisfying λ ≤ K ≤ Λ on B(x0,4r0). Then for any r > 0 with r ≤ r0 (and r ≤ π/(4√Λ) if Λ>0) the injectivity radius at x0 is bounded below by
inj(M,x0) ≥ r · Vol(B(x0,r)) / (Vol(B(x0,r)) + V^n_λ(2r)),
where V^n_λ(2r) is the volume of a radius 2r ball in the simply connected space form of constant curvature λ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local curvature upper and lower bounds on a ball of radius 4r0 plus a positive radius r produce a concrete lower bound for inj at the center in terms of the volume of the ball and the model-space volume; valid provided r does not exceed the conjugate-radius restrictions (π/(4√Λ) when Λ>0). The proof lifts to the exponential chart and compares volumes of fundamental-domain preimages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localized injectivity-radius bound under radial curvature control (Corollary 4.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If B(p0,s0) is a geodesic ball in a complete n-manifold M and for every 0<s<s0 the sectional curvature on B(p0,s) satisfies |K| ≤ Λ(s) for some positive increasing function Λ on [0,s0), then for any p with d(p0,p)=s and any r with 0<r≤(s0−s)/4 the injectivity radius inj(M,p) is bounded below by an explicit function depending only on n, inj(M,p0), Λ and s (given in the text in terms of model volumes V^n_{Λ(s+2r0)}). In particular there exists ρ_{n,δ,Λ}(s)>0 giving a uniform lower bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a way to control injectivity radius at p in terms of the basepoint injectivity radius, the radial function Λ(s) of curvature bounds, and volumes; the statement produces an explicit (though complicated) lower bound and shows injectivity radius can be controlled locally even on noncompact manifolds when curvature growth is controlled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exponential decay control of injectivity radius with distance (estimate (4.2.4))
rubrics_metrics.description:
If curvature is uniformly bounded by B and inj(M,p0) ≥ δ > 0, then for any p we have an estimate of the form
inj(M,p) ≥ (δ√B)^n e^{−C√B d(p,p0)} (up to dimensional constants),
so injectivity radius falls off at worst exponentially in distance from p0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under a uniform curvature upper bound, injectivity radius cannot decay faster than exponentially in the distance to a basepoint; constants depend only on the dimension and curvature bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Little Loop Lemma (Theorem 4.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let g_{ij}(t), 0 ≤ t < T, be a Ricci flow solution on a compact manifold M. There exists ρ>0 such that: if at (x0,t0) and on the spatial ball B_{t0}(x0,r) for times t in (t0−r^2, t0] the curvature satisfies |Rm| ≤ r^{−2} (and r ≤ √T), then the injectivity radius at x0 with respect to g_{ij}(t0) satisfies inj(M,x0,g(t0)) ≥ ρ r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a no-local-collapsing type injectivity-radius estimate along Ricci flow: uniform curvature control on a parabolic neighborhood of size r forces a uniform definite fraction of r as a lower bound on injectivity radius. It relies on Perelman's no-local-collapsing theorem and yields that short curvature scale implies definite geometric noncollapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of (almost) maximum points (Definition 4.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence (x_k,t_k) of space-time points is a sequence of (almost) maximum points if there exist positive constants c1 and α ∈ (0,1] such that |Rm(x_k,t_k)| ≥ c1 K_max(t_k) and for t in [t_k − α / K_max(t_k), t_k] the same relation (comparable size) holds (i.e., these points realize nearly maximal curvature in a controlled backward time interval).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This picks out space-time centers at (nearly) the highest curvature scales used when forming blow-up (dilation) limits; the constants c1 and α quantify how close to the global maximum the chosen points are and over what backward time window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injectivity radius condition for Ricci-flow sequences (Definition 4.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description:
A solution satisfies the injectivity radius condition if for any sequence of (almost) maximum points (x_k,t_k) there exists c2>0 (independent of k) such that
inj(M,x_k,g(t_k)) ≥ c2 / sqrt(K_max(t_k))
for all k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This condition guarantees that at the high-curvature centers used for rescaling, the injectivity radius is comparable to the curvature length scale (inverse sqrt of curvature), preventing collapse at the rescaling scale and enabling application of compactness theorems to obtain nontrivial limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of maximal Ricci-flow solutions (Type I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Type I maximal solution: T < +∞ and sup_{t∈[0,T)} (T−t) K_max(t) < +∞ (i.e., curvature blows up at most at rate (T−t)^{−1}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type I captures finite-time singularities where curvature growth is at most the canonical rate; these are the classical Type I blow-up regime and are amenable to parabolic rescaling to obtain shrinking soliton limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of maximal Ricci-flow solutions (Type II)
rubrics_metrics.description: Type II solutions are those not Type I; split into: (a) T < +∞ but sup_{t∈[0,T)} (T−t) K_max(t) = +∞ (faster-than-Type-I blow-up), or (b) T = +∞ but sup_{t∈[0,∞)} t K_max(t) = +∞ (curvature decays too slowly in infinite time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type II captures singularities with faster curvature blow-up than Type I (finite-time) or unbounded tK_max(t) at infinite time. Type II rescalings typically lead to steady soliton limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of maximal Ricci-flow solutions (Type III)
rubrics_metrics.description: Type III solutions: T = +∞ and sup_{t∈[0,∞)} t K_max(t) < +∞; further split into (a) lim sup_{t→∞} t K_max(t) > 0, and (b) lim sup_{t→∞} t K_max(t) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type III corresponds to long-time solutions whose curvature decays at least like 1/t; case (a) yields nontrivial expanding-type blow-up limits, while (b) is incompatible with the injectivity-radius condition except for the flat/trivial solutions under typical hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of singularity models (Definition 4.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the canonical curvature bounds that characterize the three model types one expects as blow-up limits after appropriate parabolic rescalings centered at almost-maximum points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of dilation limits to singularity models (Theorem 4.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any maximal solution satisfying the injectivity-radius condition and of Type I, II(a)/(b), or III(a), there exists a sequence of dilations around (almost) maximum points which converges in C^∞_{loc} to a singularity model of the corresponding type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the precise criterion/method to produce nontrivial limiting models (shrinking/steady/expanding) via rescaling at high-curvature points, contingent on the injectivity-radius noncollapse condition so Hamilton compactness applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonnegative-curvature variants: convergence to singularity models (Corollary 4.3.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For complete maximal solutions with bounded nonnegative curvature operator (or Kähler with nonnegative holomorphic bisectional curvature), there exist dilations along almost-maximum points converging to a singularity model; in these cases curvature can be controlled by scalar curvature up to dimension-dependent factors and the same typewise conclusions hold (Type I→shrinking, Type II→steady, Type III→expanding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonnegativity of curvature operator or holomorphic bisectional curvature simplifies curvature control and ensures the existence of model limits in the listed types; the limits are again Ricci solitons in the positive-Ricci case (see next item).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of Type II and Type III singularity models with positive Ricci curvature (Theorem 4.3.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) Any Type II singularity model with nonnegative curvature operator and positive Ricci curvature must be a steady Ricci soliton. (ii) Any Type III singularity model with nonnegative curvature operator and positive Ricci curvature must be a homothetically expanding Ricci soliton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under nonnegativity of the curvature operator (and positivity of Ricci), the limiting singularity models have the rigid structure of Ricci solitons of the appropriate (steady/expanding) type; the proof uses Li–Yau–Hamilton inequalities and maximum-principle arguments on evolved curvature quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type I compact rescaling limits are shrinking gradient solitons (Sesum Theorem 4.3.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a Type I singularity model is obtained as a rescaling limit of a Type I maximal solution and the limit manifold M is compact, then the limit must be a gradient shrinking Ricci soliton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Type I assumption controls Perelman's µ-functional making it uniformly bounded and, together with compactness of the rescaling limit, one obtains convergence of the minimizers and hence the shrinking-gradient-soliton structure for the limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradient steady Ricci-soliton identity and convexity (Lemma 4.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a complete gradient steady Ricci soliton with bounded curvature, positive Ricci curvature, and scalar curvature R attaining its maximum R_max at x0, one has |∇F|^2 + R = R_max everywhere; moreover F is convex and attains its minimum at x0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an identity tying the potential function F to scalar curvature for steady gradient solitons; it yields convexity and rigidity properties of F that are used to analyze global geometry of the soliton (e.g., exhaustion properties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymptotic scalar curvature ratio for steady gradient solitons (Theorem 4.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a complete noncompact steady gradient Ricci soliton with bounded curvature and positive sectional curvature where scalar curvature attains its maximum at some point O, the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio A = lim sup_{s→∞} R s^2 equals +∞ (i.e., Rs^2 → +∞ along some sequence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes that scalar curvature does not decay faster than s^{-2} at infinity (indeed grows in the s^2-weighted sense), an important gap-type result for positively curved steady solitons, and is used to rule out certain flat limits when flowing backwards in time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of 2D complete steady Ricci soliton with bounded curvature (Theorem 4.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only complete steady Ricci soliton on a two-dimensional manifold with bounded curvature which attains its scalar-curvature maximum 1 at an origin is the cigar soliton on R^2 with metric ds^2 = (dx^2+dy^2)/(1+x^2+y^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof uses that the soliton is a gradient soliton, conformal vector-field analysis in complex coordinates, convexity properties of the potential, and asymptotic expansions to identify the metric uniquely as the cigar soliton.
